articles.title: Fridge freezers left at Newport Docks amid suspended collections
articles.summary: A recycling firm collapsed in 2025, leaving the appliances in limbo until a takeover is complete.
articles.body:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

Lee said he was also confused by the different policies in neighbouring councils.

"If I lived in Barry or Penarth (Vale of Glamorgan) they would be able to collect it from the kerb. I don't know why I can't in Cardiff."

The Welsh Local Government Association has been asked why some councils are still able to carry out the collections while others are not.

Michael Enea, a campaigner in Newport who blogs about fly-tipping, said he often saw the old appliances at the side of the road and thinks this could now get worse.

"I think there'll be a lot of people in local communities where they don't have the ability to dispose of their fridges and freezers, who will end up literally dumping them in the street.

"We see it quite a lot in Newport and right over Wales."

The LGA said it had identified dozens of councils across Wales and England that had been forced to stop or restrict collections, with more expected to follow suit.

Oxfordshire County Council has urged the UK government to reopen the Newport plant to help with the "crisis".

Associated British Ports, which took over the running of the Newport site, said it was "in discussions with third parties" about the future of the site and materials.

A spokesperson added: "In the interim, the material is being managed responsibly as part of the site's transition and will be transferred to another specialist recycling operation in due course."

Dr David Santillo, a research scientist at Greenpeace, said it was possible that some of the fridges and freezers at Newport Docks still contained "some of the most harmful chemicals" such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs).

HFCs are mainly used in air conditioning, industrial chillers and fridges, but are also powerful greenhouse gases.

Chemicals such as isobutane, pentane and ammonia can also be found in commercial-type fridges, Dr Santillo added.

"None of these chemicals are benign. They all have the potential for harmful effects, or they can be toxic if they leak," he said.

Santillo said some older chemicals could have a "much wider impact" on the environment and leaving appliances out for long periods had the potential to produce "toxic smoke" if a fire breaks out.

Santillo said the recycling of fridges and freezers was a national issue and he urged the UK government to "step in and find a solution".

Defra said it appreciated the "challenges" facing local authorities, and was working to manage the impact of treatment capacity shortages.

It added: "This includes allowing the storage of fridge and cooling equipment on temporary sites provided certain conditions set out by the Environment Agency are met."

Regulator Natural Resources Wales said it was "aware of the pressures" affecting operators across the UK.

It added that it was providing "regulatory flexibility" to help manage temporary storage pressures and would "continue to support efforts across the sector to restore treatment capacity and minimise disruption".

The Welsh government said it was working with NRW, local authorities and the UK government to "manage the situation and support a return to normal capacity."

articles.title: Strictly is back with new hosts as celebrities discover pairings
articles.summary: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over from long-running presenting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.
articles.body:
Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.

Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.

A fresh cohort of famous faces – including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips – also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.

During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.

Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour".

"Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.

In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced.

Reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin

Hair stylist to the stars Chris Appleton and Amy Dowden

Australian singer and actress Delta Goodrem and Kai Widdrington

DJ and social media personality Cach Mercer and Maddie Ingoldsby

TV and radio presenter Will Best and Dianne Buswell

Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon

TV and stage actress Bethany Antonia and Nancy Xu

Former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr

Presenter and author Graeme Hall and Lauren Oakley

Skeleton athlete Tabby Stoecker and Mark Karmalita

TV and stage actress Melanie Walters and Aljaž Škorjanec

One pair who won't need to get to know each other are reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin.

Dyer is back to compete for a second time, having withdrawn from last year's series due to a fractured ankle.

"I'm just over the moon. I'm so, so happy," she said after the pairing, while Kuzmin added that he had "tears of joy" in his eyes.

Meanwhile, actress Bethany Antonia and professional Nancy Xu became the third two-woman couple to compete in the show.

In a poignant moment, Antonia revealed that watching boxer Nicola Adams and Katya Jones performing together in Strictly's 2020 series was a "big part of my coming out journey".

Among the other pairings were EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola, former Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon, and Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr.

Also back on the dancefloor for a final spin was reigning Strictly champion, former Lionness Karen Carney.

Clad in the same diamante-encrusted football shirt, Carney recreated the Jive that first marked her out as a contender of her series, alongside dance partner Carlos Gu.

"I absolutely feel like I'm at home," Carney told Willis after the routine, as she paid tribute to her pro partner.

In 13 weeks time, she'll have to surrender that glitterball trophy to a new victor.

And it is not just presenters and celebrities navigating the ballroom for the first time: Aleksandra Isaeva, Cristian Priori, Lethabo Monametsi, Maddie Ingoldsby, and Mark Karmalita are the five new professionals joining the Strictly cast this series.

They hail from the UK, Canada, Italy, South Africa and Ukraine.

The five made a high-impact entrance, performing a searing routine that kicked off on top of an enormous encaged disco ball.

Saturday's show was a more paired back role for Craig Revel Horwood and his fellow judges - Motsi Mabuse, Shirley Ballas and Anton Du Beke - who featured less.

But there was still time for resident villain Horwood to direct a jibe at broadcaster Will Best's hip action: "Call in the paramedics darling, dislocation - my goodness."

And some other traditions remain intact.

Once all the dance routines were wrapped, the pairings announced, and the chats in the "Clauditorium" concluded, it was time for the show's three new hosts to bid farewell with the customary order to "staaart dancing!"

articles.title: The deadly new drugs reshaping fight against addiction
articles.summary: Experts warn potent new substances are making an already deadly crisis more dangerous.
articles.body:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

Unlike heroin or cocaine, which are derived from cultivated plants, many of the new substances are manufactured in clandestine laboratories.

They include synthetic opioids such as nitazenes and orphines, some of which are hundreds of times more potent than heroin.

Police say organised crime groups are increasingly mixing the substances with existing drugs to maximise their profits.

"I think it's shameful behaviour that we're seeing from these organised crime groups," Supt Niven Bull, of Police Scotland, said.

"They are profiting from people's misery."

On average, a new psychoactive substance emerged every week in 2025, according to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA).

The agency says tighter controls imposed by China and the Taliban's ban on poppy cultivation in Afghanistan have pushed production closer to consumer markets.

That includes Scotland, where police have raided two suspected nitazene factories in the past 14 months, making five arrests in total.

In July 2025, officers discovered an alleged illicit drugs laboratory in Patna, Ayrshire, leading to the arrest of three people.

Deputy Chief Constable Jane Connors later described it as the UK's first suspected nitazene laboratory.

BBC News can also reveal that two men, aged 43 and 56, were arrested in February this year after police searched a unit in Loanhead, Midlothian, as part of an investigation into another suspected synthetic opioid lab.

In 2024, nitazenes were implicated in 76 drug-related deaths in Scotland, according to official figures , more than three times the number of the previous year.

"These drugs are extremely dangerous, and it's pretty rapid for us to be able to keep up as scientists," says Dr Nisbet, whose laboratory is soon set to take on an expanded role as Scotland's national drug testing facility.

The changing nature of the supply also creates challenges for lawmakers who are in a race to identify and ban dangerous new substances before they can spread legally and cause havoc.

"New and harmful substances continue to be created to circumvent legal controls," EUDA points out.

While control of illicit drugs is reserved to Westminster under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, responsibility for public health, policing and prosecutions is devolved to the Scottish government and its agencies.

On the front line of the battle to save lives, charity workers say they are seeing the devastating impact of the new synthetic opioids first-hand.

In the woods at Glenbarr on the Kintyre peninsula, staff from the drug, alcohol and mental health charity With You are trying to treat trauma in a group designed to help former drug and alcohol users reconnect with nature.

Gareth Balmer, the charity's national harm reduction lead, says nitazenes and other synthetic opioids are now appearing across the drug supply, from benzodiazepine (street Valium) pills and cannabinoids, known as spice, to cocaine and heroin.

"This is a frightening new landscape," he said. "I don't think drugs have ever been as risky or as dangerous as they are now."

The result is that some users are experiencing unexpected and sometimes catastrophic overdoses.

"Some of these substances are so potent that a grain would be enough to take somebody over," Balmer warned, adding that access to naloxone, which can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, is now more important than ever.

The figures behind Scotland's drug death toll

Scottish drug deaths fall but remain worst in Europe

Bull said Police Scotland was taking a twin-track approach, promising to "relentlessly pursue" dealers while also recognising that many drug users need help.

In 2025, officers seized about £80m worth of street drugs. So far this year that figure has already reached £78m.

"Hundreds of individuals have been arrested, and many people are serving custodial sentences," Bull said.

But he added that the force also wanted to help users "to make better life choices".

"If we come across people who are suffering from addiction, who are in a low point in their life, then we will look to help support them and we'll look to refer them to the relevant agency," he said.

Prof Niamh Nic Daeid, director of Dundee University's Leverhulme laboratory, said its expanded role as a national drug testing and research centre would make a difference too.

On one hand, she said, her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities, allowing them to make safer and more informed choices. On the other, the research will help to inform government policy.

"Drugs are changing all the time," she said. "Part of the establishment of this facility is to have a research capability that will enable us to try to keep up.

"If we don't know what substances are present in the samples, how can we provide the right advice?"

Back in Kintyre, Vicky Gamble, whose own struggles with alcohol, drugs and crime have seen her in and out of prison, is enjoying the tranquillity of the forest.

She is personally hopeful of a better future but she is worried about the emerging threat of new substances and the potential effect on friends and family.

"It seems that there's a lot of stuff that all the young ones seem to be taking now and I don't even think they know what it is," she told me.

For Gareth Balmer of With You, that uncertainty is part of the danger.

He says: "It's a terrible thing to say, but with heroin it was better the devil you knew."

articles.title: Eritrea's G-15 political prisoners: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive'
articles.summary: The children of key politicians jailed 25 years ago without a trace in Eritrea want answers.
articles.body:
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.

"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.

Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.

Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.

After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.

That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.

Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.

Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.

It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.

In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.

Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.

The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.

It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.

"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.

"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."

In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.

After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.

Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.

"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.

"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"

Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.

Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.

"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."

Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.

All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.

The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.

Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.

At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.

The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.

Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.

Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.

As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."

She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.

On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."

One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.

She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.

Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.

Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.

"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.

He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.

His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.

Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.

Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.

Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.

They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.

"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.

"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.

Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.

Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.

President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.

Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.

"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."

Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.

"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.

"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."

Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.

"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

articles.title: Morning-after pills may get 4 boxed warnings
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Morning-after pills containing levonorgestrel may soon carry four prominent boxed warnings. Govt has proposed that the pills should be labe.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Morning-after pills containing levonorgestrel may soon carry four prominent boxed warnings. Govt has proposed that the pills should be labelled clearly as meant only for emergency use, not as regular contraception, not as abortion pills and not as protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections.The proposed warnings will also caution that frequent use may lead to side effects and advise users seeking regular contraception to visit a health facility or a registered medical practitioner.Dr Megha Tiwari, Consultant, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Kailash Hospital & Neuro Institute, said emergency contraceptive pills are an important and safe option when used appropriately, but concerns arise when they start being treated as routine contraception. "We do see women taking it repeatedly after unprotected intercourse, sometimes without understanding that it can disturb the menstrual cycle and cause temporary bleeding irregularities, nausea or anxiety around a delayed period," she said."The bigger issue is misinformation. Some women believe the pill can terminate an existing pregnancy, while others assume it offers protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections, which it does not," Tiwari said. She added that the proposed warnings were less about creating fear around emergency contraception and more about ensuring women understood its correct role as a backup method after contraceptive failure, rather than a replacement for regular contraception or condoms.The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed the changes through a draft amendment to Drugs Rules, 1945, covering levonorgestrel tablets of 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg. The warnings would have to appear prominently both on the packaging and the package insert.The proposal also seeks to add levonorgestrel tablets 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg as a specific entry under Schedule K of Drugs Rules, along with conditions relating to their exemption from sale-licence requirements.However, the warnings are not yet mandatory. articles.title: Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
articles.summary: Unprepared and in flip-flops, the 47-year-old widow ran 3km to try secure her daughter's future.
articles.body:
Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August.

The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education.

When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters.

It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination.

But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny.

"Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked.

Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life.

For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple.

"My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district.

"I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education."

Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books.

"I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race."

When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category.

Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous.

Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012.

"I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it."

She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had.

"I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education."

That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense.

One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job.

Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities.

The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system.

For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day.

After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment.

Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees.

But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges.

"If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak."

For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future.

"I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same."

articles.title: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice
articles.summary: A cauldron of conflicts is bubbling across the world, with cultural monuments being destroyed. These people are fighting against it.
articles.body:
August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House.

It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance.

In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa.

Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued.

Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will."

Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does.

The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage.

Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque.

The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas.

Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present."

The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep.

This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war.

In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again.

More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan.

The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush.

Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation.

In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954.

It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it.

Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage.

A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way.

When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes.

But this has been a complex and difficult task.

So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison.

Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself.

"For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously."

In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared?

In an isolated position in open countryside, a museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed by Russian shelling during an overnight attack in 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said it had left him speechless: "Targeted strikes against museums - not even terrorists would think of this. But this is the kind of army we are fighting against."

The building was set ablaze and a caretaker was injured, but much of the collection had already been removed.

Joe Biden, then the US president, said that Russian President Vladimir Putin was not only trying to take over Ukraine, but "literally trying to wipe out the culture and identity of the Ukrainian people".

That pattern has been repeated across much of the frontline in Ukraine where local organisations have worked with international groups to try to safeguard their national heritage from Russian attack.

One international group that's played a big role is the Aliph Foundation, which was set up in Geneva in 2017 to protect and repair cultural heritage.

Alexandra Fiebig, a project manager with Aliph, says that her group provided millions of dollars in funds to Ukrainian museums scrambling to move their most valuable items to safety.

This has involved the use of what she describes as 'heritage ambulances': "These vehicles that have specialised equipment and space with specialised teams and equipment, they were in the beginning travelling a lot to affected museums that were damaged through military action."

Now, she says the teams also check on the artefacts that were transported in great haste to safer places to make sure they remain in good condition.

Blue Shield International is a group that operates in multiple war zones, working with armed forces and local heritage officials to such an extent that it's come to be known as the Red Cross for culture.

Dr Emma Cunliffe, the head of operations for the group, says Ukrainians are risking their lives to protect their heritage.

"They are taking great measures to document the damage even when they are risking their own lives to do it. In fact one of the things we really see is that the government is taking huge steps despite the many many competing priorities and the struggles they are facing."

Other conflicts have seen civilians take similar measures to protect their culture.

In February 2015, Isis turned its attention from hacking down ancient statues and artefacts in Mosul in northern Iraq to ransacking its written heritage as its fighters laid waste to the city's much treasured public libraries. They burned the Central Library and destroyed or stole many thousands of books - many of them rare manuscripts that told the story of the city.

"These were not simply books or shelves, they represented decades of knowledge and research and formed an important part of the intellectual heritage of Mosul University and the wider community… Within days, everything was gone," Dr Mohammed Jasim Mohammed al-Hamdani says. The main library in Mosul has played a key role in his life - to such an extent that he is now the director there.

"Seeing it destroyed felt like losing a part of myself. Many people in the city had a story connected to the University of Mosul and therefore the loss felt very close to home. And this is why when that part of Mosul was liberated from Isis, young people, old people rushed to the library to save what they could."

The obverse of communities taking it into their own hands to protect cultural property is the looting of those same sites.

Again, this is a byproduct of war that dates back to the dawn of history.

Cunliffe says that understanding the reasons for looting - which can vary from place to place - is a necessary starting point: "That might then in turn result in greater sanctions, greater prosecutions to take it seriously as a threat." She says that it's important if possible to convey a sense to local communities that by assisting this, they are selling their own heritage.

In Iraq and Syria for example, both during and after the Isis rampage, looting of priceless artefacts was carried out on an industrial scale.

The precious objects were spirited out and trafficked abroad, including to the US.

A years-long investigation by the US Justice Department traced and tracked the smuggling routes and resulted in thousands of looted artefacts being returned to Iraq.

In Europe and elsewhere, co-ordinated, multi-national police and customs operations take place regularly, seizing large numbers of stolen antiquities and arresting some of the traffickers.

But the trade remains highly lucrative and the plethora of conflicts provides ever more opportunities.

In Sudan, the national museum in Khartoum was stripped of its treasures in 2023 when it came under the control of one of the warring factions, the RSF, which loaded them onto trucks and left the display rooms bare.

As in other conflict zones like Ukraine, specialised training has been provided for those involved in trying to recover the antiquities, which has had some success. But much of the museum's display - which told the story of the region over thousands of years - may have disappeared for good.

The challenges of trying to limit the scale of destruction and looting of cultural heritage are huge.

At an international or state level, there are regulations in place, but putting them into practice in a timely fashion is difficult enough - and often there isn't even the will to attempt this.

Local initiatives backed by organisations like Aliph and Blue Shield International can make a difference on a small scale.

But if - as seems the case right now - the chances of anyone facing consequences for destroying a heritage site are close to zero, then there is all but no real deterrent.

"What would change the calculation is not harsher sentences," says Dr Bijan Rouhani, "but a real prospect of being named - arrest warrants for the commanders who authorise these strikes, prosecutions in national courts under universal jurisdiction, and targeted sanctions on named individuals. Those measures don't require a new treaty. They require states to be willing to use the instruments they already have, against allies as well as adversaries."

Of all the recent attempts to erase the cultural past embodied in stone, Palmyra in Syria still stands out. Isis blew up temples there and might have done far worse if it had not been defeated.

One man became emblematic for standing up to them. For 40 years, the archaeologist Khaled al-Asaad had been the principal custodian of Palmyra. He was in his eighties when Isis descended on the ancient city.

They captured him and tortured him to try to find out where its most valuable artefacts had been hidden. When he refused to tell them, they beheaded him in a public square and hung his corpse from a traffic light.

Al-Asaad was celebrated across the world as a heroic defender of culture against the forces of darkness. He was awarded the Order of Civil Merit in Syria and in Palmyra, a school was named in his honour.

But nothing is free from political complications.

Years later, under the new authorities in Syria, his name has now been removed from the school.

articles.title: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth
articles.summary: "It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," Horgan reveals.
articles.body:
Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.

Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.

The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too.

And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.

I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters.

"We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, an… autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"

The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.

The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son".

Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent".

"And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"

But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work.

"I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says.

"I try to put all that in there… and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."

She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.

The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy.

"This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.

There are new issues to concern ourselves with in mid-life and, as you'd expect, Horgan doesn't shy away from embarrassing situations or mildly unhealthy preoccupations.

Her protagonist - who is 50 - has a slight obsession with sagging skin, which will no doubt strike a chord with many.

"It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," she reveals.

Horgan says she wanted to offer "an honest depiction of someone having a complicated relationship with ageing". She adds that she herself has now formed "a better relationship" with getting older.

"I think it's OK to age any way you want to age. And we're insecure about it for a reason. And that's because it's shoved down our necks that we need to look a certain way, especially within the entertainment industry and in magazines. And women who age really well are celebrated just for that. And that is annoying."

When it comes to sex, she says "you just have different insecurities" when you're a bit older.

"You think about angles, you think about the shapes you make and how to be sexy as an older woman. And, you, know, lighting comes into it! But I also have friends who are incredibly free with their bodies and feel like this is a whole new era and they're embracing it.

"I know that I will get there," she continues. "But I wanted to show a middle-aged woman having a complicated relationship with her body but still putting herself out there because... she wants to find someone to grow old with."

Sherwood star Sharlene Whyte, who plays Horgan's boss and best friend Sam, says we need to see older women's stories on screen.

"We should see more of it - women who are later on in age, who have been privileged to get here later on, who are still killing it and are still beautiful and sexy and funny," she says.

"But I think women in their 50s are more visible (now)... and there's more (acting) work for women in later life."

Despite the two lead characters being 50-something women, Whyte describes Youth as "an inter-generational watch".

That's probably due to a prominent Gen Z storyline involving Alex's son, Ruari, played by 19-year-old Aran Murphy (Cillian Murphy's son. And yes, as you might expect, he's very good).

Ruari has a difficult relationship with his feckless father - Alex's ex-husband (Owen McDonnell) - and in one poignant scene, describes how confusing it is to find your way as a young man in today's world.

"Having good people around you is so important, and it's not always easy to have that," Murphy muses.

"So, for someone like Ruari, when you don't have the foundation of friends and stuff, you look to the (wrong) kinds of people... and oftentimes, you'll be left out on your ass with the wrong answers."

What does he hope young people who might catch the show will take away from it?

"You don't have to have it all in place at 18, everyone is still kind of just pretending they know what they're doing."

I suggest that we don't always know what we're doing in later life either.

He laughs. "Exactly. Everyone's still figuring it out."

Youth will debut on 21 September in the UK & Ireland on HBO Max.

articles.title: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity
articles.summary: A report suggests older LGBTQ+ people experience more social isolation than their heterosexual peers.
articles.body:
As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.

But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.

She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.

The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.

Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation.

"It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says.

"In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."

He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.

Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.

The scheme, a joint project with the local council, will provide 80 self-contained apartments and communal areas available to the local community.

The majority of residents will be LGBTQ+.

The Kindred House scheme is what's known as extra-care housing, which means residents live independently, but there is a 24/7 care team available for those who need extra help, and all staff will receive specialist training around LGBTQ+ inclusion.

Porter says he hopes the scheme will "trigger some conversations" about how to best support older LGBTQ+ people in the challenges they face.

'People start clumping you together with other stereotypes'

Mindy and her wife Linda have been together for more than 30 years, but says they're often mistaken for sisters.

"She's 18 inches taller than me, I've got a Yorkshire accent and she's got a Northern Irish accent," Mindy says. "I think it's pretty obvious we weren't brought up in the same building."

She believes part of that is often down to people presuming she is straight because of her age.

"There are different tribes of people in every age group, but when you get older, people start clumping you together with other stereotypes," she says.

On one occasion, while Mindy was in hospital after a stroke, a nurse referred to Linda as Mindy's husband. She said it was not only "insulting", but made her consider what sort of training the staff might have had.

The Spotlight on Ageing report says these sort of experiences can also have an impact on the support people receive.

Sarah Wilkinson, research and analysis manager at the Centre for Ageing Better, says after a "lifetime of homophobia and transphobia", older LGBTQ+ people now face the "additional, and overlapping, challenge of ageism".

The report says older LGBTQ+ people are less likely to have children - someone born in 1950 would have been in their 50s by the time same-sex couples could legally adopt - and that they are more likely to be estranged from their families when compared to their heterosexual counterparts.

The report also found more than half of gay and bisexual men aged 65 and above live alone, compared with less than a quarter of heterosexual men. Bisexual women aged 50 to 64 are twice as likely as their heterosexual peers to live alone.

It also suggests that only half of gay and bisexual men aged 50 and above definitely agree they would have someone to help them if they needed, 14 percentage points lower than heterosexual men of the same age.

Norman Goodman, 75, came out as bisexual in his late 60s after the death of his wife Marilyn.

The couple never had children, and Norman now has no immediate family nearby to help him with things like hospital visits or housework.

He says his support system comes in the form of his partner Tony, and a group of friends and neighbours he refers to as his "chosen family".

"I'm lucky, I've got great friends and great neighbours, and I know I can knock on somebody's door day or night and I could get help," he says.

But despite having their support while he's relatively independent, Norman says he worries about the prospect of facing discrimination if he needs more formal care as he ages.

"Hopefully I will maintain and look after myself the best I can, but I've heard horror stories of gay people in nursing homes being treated terribly," he says.

"I think nurses, doctors, carers should all be trained on how to look after LGBT people."

It's the reason behind schemes like Manchester's Kindred House, which are not unusual in other parts of the world.

There are similar projects in Spain, Sweden, Germany, the US and Canada, but in the UK they are few and far between.

In 2021, the UK's first LGBTQ+ retirement home, Tonic, opened in London with 19 apartments for private rental or shared ownership.

The scheme attracted so much attention, later this year it is set to feature in a Netflix documentary telling the story of one of its first residents, Chek Min-Ong.

After 43 years together, Min, 77, and his late partner Tim, had discussed their plans for a future where one of them would live alone, as Tim's health deteriorated.

"Tim and I have always had this very open discussion, we wanted to know, when one of us is not here anymore, the other person will have a community and feel safe," Min says.

When Tim died five months after moving into Tonic, Min says his new-found community rallied around him.

"It is what [Tim and I] always wanted, that we'd never have to explain ourselves," he says. "We'd never have to face a question and feel guilty about not telling the full story, or having to lie.

'It's something I'm really proud to be a part of'

While schemes like Kindred House and Tonic are welcomed by Mindy, Norman and Min, the Spotlight on Ageing report warns that, because the older LGBTQ+ population is growing, the demand for specialist services is expected to outstrip supply.

Between 2019 and 2024, the number of over-50s identifying as lesbian, gay or bisexual in the UK increased by around a third - from roughly 340,000 to almost 460,000.

There was a 4% rise in the number of heterosexual people aged 50 and above in the same period.

These numbers are projected to continue to increase as the relatively larger younger generations of people identifying as LGBTQ+ age.

Porter warns that without more schemes like Kindred House, and more training and awareness for those in other care settings, the ageing population may struggle to get proper support.

For Mindy, who is part of a steering group advising on the plans, knowing there may be more options available in the future is reassuring.

"It's important that you can go, that you think, 'You know what, I could live there because I know the staffing, the ethics, the rules, everything about the place has been put together from an LGBTQ+ focus,'" she says.

"That's what we've been doing and it's something I'm really proud of being a part of."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia claims Houthis tried to attack its capital Riyadh with missiles
articles.summary: Middle East News: Saudi Arabia said Saturday that Yemen’s Houthis attempted to strike Riyadh with a ballistic missile, marking the first reported attack on the capital .
articles.body: Saudi Arabia said Saturday that Yemen’s Houthis attempted to strike Riyadh with a ballistic missile, marking the first reported attack on the capital since fighting with the Iran-backed group intensified amid the wider Iran war.The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted the missile. Residents reported hearing an explosion, while a plume of smoke was later seen near the airport. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage, reported AP.The coalition also said Houthi attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, as well as Taif, Baysh and Farasan, were thwarted.The Houthis claimed they had targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in Yanbu, alleging that the attacks caused “massive fires”.Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group had used cruise and ballistic missiles and drones. He also accused Saudi Arabia of attempting to strike the rebel-held Yemeni capital Sanaa.The latest escalation follows a series of Houthi attacks in recent days. Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that it intercepted a Houthi drone targeting Mecca, while on Thursday its civil defence said debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed a Yemeni resident in Saudi Arabia.The developments come as fighting has also intensified inside Yemen, where the Houthis have advanced along the Red Sea coast and seized the port city of Mokha and islands near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.Regional officials told AP that Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has sought air-defence support from France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Candace Owens has opened another line of questioning in the Charlie Kirk murder case, this time focusing on footage from a 2022 car crash involving Tyler Robinson. A viral social media post has drawn attention to her latest remarks, in which she questions why the recording surfaced after Robinson became a suspect. Her comments followed YouTuber Zach Costello's observation about Robinson's body language in the video.Candace Owens questions Tyler Robinson’s 2022 crash footageOwens said Costello's analysis prompted her to look beyond the similarities in Robinson's movements and question how the footage reached the public. She suggested that its timing deserved scrutiny, although she did not provide evidence of a coordinated effort to release it."Moving on from that, I have a random bee in my bonnet today. I need your help, internet. It's bothering me tremendously.I can't let it go suddenly. Actually, credit to YouTuber Zach Costello for putting this bee in my bonnet, even though he didn't mean to. Basically, what happened was he was looking at the footage that we released of Tyler Robinson, in the American shirt, walking onto UVU campus.He was addressing how he had his fingers in his pockets and the way that he was particularly holding his fingers in his pockets. In Zach Costello's mind, he said, that's super interesting because that makes me think of that 2022 arrest of Tyler Robinson. He also had his fingers in the pocket that way.But of course, my crazy brain, instead of hearing what Zach Costello is saying, which is like, this could be Tyler Robinson, I went, whoa, whoa, whoa. Wait a second. Why the heck did we ever see that footage? Let me back this up for you.The footage itself is now exceedingly problematic. Why and who collected and stored this footage? We can now watch a little clip of it, just so you can see what we're referring to, because I don't think we actually ever talked about it on this show."Owens then played a clip of an officer speaking with a driver after a collision. The exchange appears routine, with the driver explaining how the crash happened. Owens questioned why the recording remained available years later."Who's the driver? You're the driver? Yep.Can you tell me just really quick what happened?I was coming this way and he was just passing through and he pulled out from here or no, from there, I think.Do you remember which lane you were in?I was in one of those two lanes going this way, I think in the right.Yeah. In the right most lane coming this way. Okay. And he would have been there going left.And as I was coming through, he turned in and I T-boned into the side.Okay.Mundane.I'm going to keep asking this. Who requested and stored this footage for three years and then submitted it to Scripps News? Who in Utah was like, I happen to have this footage from 2022 that I've been holding on to of this random, unknown 19-year-old Tyler Robinson, and I'm choosing to release it to a publication that no one has ever heard of."Candace Owens connects footage release to wider Charlie Kirk case questionsOwens compared the footage's release to what she described as the repeated use of maroon shirts in coverage of Robinson. She also questioned whether the similarities in his clothing were meant to shape public perception. These suggestions remain her claims, not established findings."Because you want to know what I think? I think this is like the maroon shirts. When I suddenly said, every news organization was showing us pictures of Tyler in a maroon shirt. And you would think that he always wore maroon shirts, but he didn't actually. He normally wore blue shirts.And it seems like they knew that some decoys were going to wear the maroon shirt and they wanted to immediately imprint upon the public's mind that Tyler just wore maroon every day. They didn't.I think this is similar. I think that they already knew they were going to release this to the public and they had trained this individual to mimic the way in which Tyler Robinson walks. I think that because the New York Post kind of said that, right? When they released the footage, they were basically like, wow, shocking footage emerges of Tyler Robinson. And he's wearing an eerily similar hat and sunglasses from the 2022 footage."Owens continued by challenging the circumstances surrounding the video's release and asking viewers to share information about its handling."Look, it's just unbelievable. This fender bender in Utah, sporting sunglasses and a hat that are eerily similar to what he was seen wearing while on the run after allegedly gunning down conservative activist, Charlie Kirk, three years later. Wow. How crazy that this footage emerged and he's in the same hat and sunglasses imprinting upon the public mind that this is our guy. That's my thought.I would like to know why footage that did not involve a crime was available on the ready a couple of days after we learned, seven days after we learned that Tyler Robinson was a suspect. How did scripts get that?If you have information as to how that took place, who held onto that footage, why they held onto that footage, which should have been deleted after 60 days in the state of Utah, which no one should have requested because no one should have known that it happened. Please reach out to us. We'd like to, we'd like to, it's, it's, it's a bee in my bonnet and my bonnets got to get to the bottom of it. It's more tips at Candace Owens.com."She closed by floating further possibilities without presenting evidence to support them."Thank you, Zach Castello for putting this bee in my bonnet. I know you were thinking a different route, but I'm always like that men in black scene where like, you know, I go after the girl. There's all these aliens and I, my brain just works different way. And now this has to be solved more tips at Candace Owens.com or you can email us at tips at Candace Owens.com.Maybe you work for scripts. Maybe, you know how they got this footage. Maybe you work for St. George, you know, who works for St. George and could have maybe held onto this footage. Maybe it's a whole blackmail thing. I don't know. They're in a gifted program and they're like, we got to anything we find about this. But I didn't Mike Mitchell. Wasn't he his mentor? Would he have maybe opened up to someone and said, Hey, I just got pulled over. I don't know. It's weird. It's all very weird. We'll be right back after a brief break."Owens' remarks add another layer to the online debate surrounding the case. However, questions about the footage's retention and release do not, by themselves, establish evidence of manipulation or a planned operation.
